opus-5.5.text:
Yeah, that's a really interesting question, and honestly it's one of the directions I'm most excited about. In most of our experiments so far we start from some initial program, often a fairly simple baseline that already does something reasonable for the task. That gives the evolutionary process a foothold: the LLM mutation operators can make targeted edits, we evaluate, and the archive gradually fills with better and more diverse solutions.

Starting from an empty program is a different regime. You're asking the system not just to refine but to bootstrap. I think there are a few ingredients that would make that work.

First, the mutation operators would have to lean much more on full rewrites and generative proposals rather than small diff-based edits. Early on there's nothing to diff against, so you want the LLM to propose whole candidate programs from the task description and the evaluation signal. Once you have a handful of rough programs, you can shift toward more local edits and crossover.

Second, the evaluation signal matters a lot. From an empty start, almost everything will fail at first, so a binary pass/fail is too sparse. You'd want shaped feedback: partial credit, intermediate metrics, even textual feedback from the evaluator that goes back into the prompt. That turns failures into useful information instead of dead ends.

Third, diversity becomes even more important. With a strong initial program, the risk is that everything collapses around that one design. From scratch, you have a chance to discover genuinely different approaches, but only if the system protects novelty. Things like novelty-based rejection sampling and island models, where subpopulations evolve somewhat independently, help keep several lineages alive long enough to mature.

And fourth, I think there's a meta-level component. The system could learn which prompting strategies or which models in the ensemble work best at different stages. Maybe one model is great at producing a first working scaffold and another is better at fine-grained optimization, and an adaptive bandit over models can figure that out online.

So the vision is open-ended discovery: you specify the problem and an evaluator, and the system builds up a whole tree of solutions, ideally including some we wouldn't have thought to write as a starting point. That's harder and more expensive, but it's closer to what we actually want from automated scientific discovery.

r001.rationale: The response describes starting from scratch with full-program proposals, then evolving multiple lineages, and says the system could build a tree of solutions.

fable-5.1.text:
Yeah, that's actually a question we've thought about quite a bit, because in principle the whole point of an evolutionary system is that you shouldn't need to hand it a good starting point. In practice, though, when we started with Shinka Evolve, we always seeded it with some initial program, even a very naive one, and the reason is that the mutation operators we use are LLM-driven. The model looks at a parent program, it looks at the fitness feedback, and it proposes an edit. If the parent is literally empty, there's nothing to edit, so the first step degenerates into something like a zero-shot "write me a solution" prompt, and you're basically just sampling from the base model at that point.

Where it gets interesting is what happens after that first generation. If you think of it in the classic evolutionary framing, you need a population, you need variation, and you need selection pressure. From an empty program, the first batch of samples is your population. They'll be very diverse, because the model isn't anchored on anything, and most of them will probably fail or get a very low score. But that's fine, because the archive keeps the ones that at least run, and now you've got a scaffold for the LLM to work from. So I'd say it's less that the system "can't" start from empty, and more that the first generation is a different regime, almost like a diversity-generation phase, and then it transitions into the refinement phase where we see most of the gains.

There are a couple of things we'd want to do to make that work well. One is to lean heavily on the novelty rejection and the embedding-based similarity we already use, because in that early phase the biggest failure mode is collapse, where the model keeps writing the same textbook solution over and over. You want to actively push the population apart. The second is that the fitness signal has to be informative when almost everything is broken. If you only get a binary pass/fail, then nothing in the first generation has gradient, so to speak. So you'd want things like partial credit, or the stdout and error traces being fed back as context, so the LLM can reason about why something failed rather than just seeing a zero.

And honestly, the thing I find most exciting is that an empty start is a nice test of how much of the final performance is coming from the base model's priors versus the evolutionary search. If you start from a strong hand-written baseline, it's hard to disentangle those. If you start from nothing and still end up with the kinds of solutions we saw on, say, the circle packing problems or the ALE-Bench tasks, that's a much stronger statement about what the search is contributing. So I'd love to see that done more systematically, and I think the infrastructure is mostly there, it's really about tuning that early phase differently from the later one.

r001.rationale: The response proposes treating the first batch of samples from an empty program as the initial population, then evolving from those branches.

astra-6.text:
I think the key question is: what does “empty” mean here? You could start with an empty program, but you still need a task description and some way of evaluating what gets generated. Those provide the signal for the search.

Then the language model proposes an initial implementation. It might be very simple, or it might not even run. You execute it, feed back the errors or the performance score, and use that information to generate the next candidates. Once you have working programs, you can start maintaining a population and exploring different directions instead of just repeatedly refining one solution.

So you wouldn’t be discovering everything from nothing. The language model brings a substantial prior about how to write programs and solve problems. The interesting question is whether the evolutionary process can take that prior and, through experimentation, find solutions that the model wouldn’t produce in a single attempt.

r001.rationale: The response says one could start with an empty program, then generate and iteratively refine candidates. It does not propose branching from that empty program as a way to explore solutions.

sol-6.1.text:
I think the interesting question is what you give it besides the empty program. You still need a task specification and some way of evaluating a candidate. If you have those, then the first step can simply be to propose a minimal working solution, get feedback, and start evolving from there.

The difficult part is that an empty program gives you very little signal. Most initial attempts might fail, and if all you return is the same bad score, there’s no direction for the search. So execution feedback—what failed, whether the output was valid, perhaps which parts of the task it solved—could be quite useful.

I’d also want to maintain multiple starting points. Rather than committing immediately to one implementation and refining it, you could explore several quite different approaches. Then evolution can work both on improving those approaches and on discovering which starting points are actually promising. You’re starting from an empty file, but the language model is still bringing a prior about what a useful program might look like.

r001.rationale: The response suggests exploring several different starting points from an empty file, rather than committing to one implementation, which communicates branching as a way to explore solutions.
